newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar likely to keep marching higher, dealers say.
newsitem.headline: Dollar likely to keep marching higher, dealers say.

text.p: The dollar has more spring left in its legs despite having already jumped to multiple-year highs against both the yen and mark, dealers said on Tuesday.
A growing disparity between a vital U.S. economy and feebler performances in Japan and Germany would continue to fuel the greenback's rise, they said.
"As far as the dollar goes, it is still strong on economic factors and likely to rise to 120 yen," said Yasuji Yamanaka, vice-president at the Bank of America in Tokyo.

The dollar's most recent surge, which sent it to a fresh 46-month high of 118.29 yen in London on Monday, was set off on Friday by the release of stronger-than-expected U.S. trade and manufacturing data.

In contrast, worries over the Japanese economy helped push Tokyo stocks into a fresh plunge of more than 600 points on Monday, while German officials have continued to express concern about their weak economy.
Tokyo's key Nikkei index fell another 122.18 points, or 0.70 percent, to 17,358.16 on Tuesday.
"Fundamentally, the economies are going to decide which way currencies trade," John Reedyk, at ANZ Bank in Melbourne, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

But a raft of comments from Japanese and U.S. authorities on Tuesday suggested that while the U.S. side may be content to let the dollar remain as it is, some Japanese officials are starting to feel enough is enough.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the current yen weakness was overdone and that Japan would take appropriate steps to combat excessive moves in currency markets.
In contrast, New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough told reporters he shares U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's stance on a strong dollar.
These comments sent the dollar bouncing from above 118 yen down to a day low of 117.55 yen and then back up again.

The dollar rose to about 118.15 yen in the late afternoon after Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was quoted as saying that he did not consider the yen's recent weakness excessive, but what was worrying were wild fluctuations in exchange rates.

"There does seem to be a bit of a difference in stances developing, with the U.S. still saying a strong dollar is good while Japan is getting concerned now," said Bank of America's Yamanaka. But he added that even the United States was likely to become worried should the dollar rise to 120 yen or above.
Most dealers agreed that 120 yen was indeed possible, perhaps even within several months.

"The near-term target against the yen is 118.60 yen, and if we can make it above that we're likely to have clear sailing up to 120 yen," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, although he noted that the upward moves were starting to be constrained near 119 yen.

There is also growing concern in the market about the chance that Japanese monetary authorities may take steps to curb the dollar's rise, perhaps even through dollar-selling intervention by the Bank of Japan. But while rumours of such moves have emerged in the past week, no concrete activity has been detected.

Although Mitsuzuka said members of the Group of Seven countries, whose finance ministers are due to meet in Berlin on February 8, would come up with a judgment on exchange rates later, other dealers felt such a consensus was unlikely.
"Unlike Japan, the Germans appear to feel happy with the current dollar/mark level," Jun Ishii, director of foreign exchange sales at SBC Warburg in Tokyo, told RFTV.
"The yen is weak, the mark and Swiss franc even weaker. Right now there's nothing to buy but the dollar," a dealer at Dresdner Bank AG in Tokyo said.
